scenes.visual: Title card 'Why Genes Keep Time' over a faint Y-shaped tree. COLOUR MAP, the same in both films: GOLD = a DNA change (a new mutation, a tick mark, a changed site); BLUE = branch and dots of species A; GREEN = branch and dots of species B; GREY = the common ancestor and unchanged sites; a brown stone icon = a fossil; CORAL = amino-acid (nonsynonymous) changes and the dN counter; TEAL = the dS counter. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Dots, trees, codon blocks and beads are simple cartoons; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. No molecular structures.

scenes.tts: Two species left no fossil of the moment they split. Can their genes still tell you when it happened? Line up the same gene from both, and some sites differ.
scenes.visual: Two cartoon animals, one BLUE, one GREEN, side by side with a question mark between them. Below each, a long horizontal gene bar of GREY squares. The two bars slide together and align; a few squares light GOLD where they differ. Label 'same gene, two species'.
scenes.narration: Two species left no fossil of the moment they split. Can their genes still tell you when it happened? Line up the same gene from both, and some sites differ.

scenes.tts: Start with one ancestral population. It splits into two lineages, and each keeps gaining mutations. Some spread until every member of the lineage carries them. A mutation that has spread like that is a substitution.
scenes.visual: A GREY circle of dots (ancestral population) at the bottom splits into two branches growing upward, BLUE left and GREEN right. Show the BLUE population as a few stacked rows, one row per generation: each new row is made of offspring of dots in the row below, and the old row fades. One dot in a row is GOLD; over several generations its GOLD descendants rise and fall in number by chance, until one row is all GOLD; at that moment a GOLD tick mark stamps onto the BLUE branch. Label on the tick: 'substitution'.
scenes.narration: Start with one ancestral population. It splits into two lineages, and each keeps gaining mutations. Some spread until every member of the lineage carries them. A mutation that has spread like that is a substitution.

scenes.tts: Substitutions build up on both branches, starting from the common ancestor. So the differences you count between two species come from both branches added together.
scenes.visual: Time scrolls upward; GOLD ticks appear on both branches at irregular moments but at the same average pace. At the two tips the gene bars light GOLD at the matching sites. A bracket joins the left ticks and the right ticks into one total labelled 'differences = ticks on BLUE branch + ticks on GREEN branch'. On screen: 'D = 2rt (same rate r on both branches)'.
scenes.narration: Substitutions build up on both branches, starting from the common ancestor. So the differences you count between two species come from both branches added together.

scenes.tts: If substitutions pile up at a steady pace, their count measures time. But why should the pace be steady at all? The answer lies inside a population.
scenes.visual: The tree shrinks to the corner. A metronome-style tick track runs along the bottom, even spacing, with a question mark over it. The camera zooms into the BLUE population circle.
scenes.narration: If substitutions pile up at a steady pace, their count measures time. But why should the pace be steady at all? The answer lies inside a population.

scenes.tts: Picture two populations, one small and one large. Every generation, each copies the same gene. Follow only the neutral mutations. They make no difference to survival or reproduction.
scenes.visual: Two boxes side by side: SMALL with 6 BLUE dots, LARGE with 24 BLUE dots, labelled 'more individuals (schematic, not to scale)' (same visual as the population-size figure). A generation counter ticks; each generation the dots are replaced by offspring of the previous generation. A tag 'neutral: no effect on survival or reproduction'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Picture two populations, one small and one large. Every generation, each copies the same gene. Follow only the neutral mutations. They make no difference to survival or reproduction.

scenes.tts: Suppose the large population were ten times bigger. It makes ten times more new mutations each generation. Does it pile up substitutions ten times faster?
scenes.visual: The LARGE box label changes to '10 x more individuals (schematic)'. New GOLD dots sparkle in both boxes each generation, many more in the large box (on screen: '10 x more new mutations'). A question appears: 'substitutions 10 x faster?' with two buttons 'yes' and 'no'.
scenes.narration: Suppose the large population were ten times bigger. It makes ten times more new mutations each generation. Does it pile up substitutions ten times faster?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: faster, or the same?'.

scenes.tts: No. Each new neutral mutation starts as one copy among many. In the large population, its chance of spreading to everyone is smaller, by the same factor. More mutations, but each one is less likely to spread.
scenes.visual: In both boxes most new GOLD dots are lost within a few generations. Beside each box runs a long tick track; GOLD substitution ticks land on it at irregular, unsynchronised moments (fixation also takes longer on average in the larger population). Small corner label: 'ideal neutral model, single-copy mutations'. On screen beside the large box: '10 x more new mutations' and 'each has 1/10 the expected fixation probability'.
scenes.narration: No. Each new neutral mutation starts as one copy among many. In the large population, its chance of spreading to everyone is smaller, by the same factor. More mutations, but each one is less likely to spread.

scenes.tts: The two effects cancel. On average, neutral mutations become substitutions at the rate they arise, whatever the population size. That steady input makes the clock tick.
scenes.visual: The two tick tracks beside the boxes stay irregular, but a running counter under each shows the same average number of ticks over a long stretch; label 'same average rate'. On screen: 'substitution rate K = mutation rate mu (neutral sites, on average)'. The metronome track returns, labelled 'clock (on average)'.
scenes.narration: The two effects cancel. On average, neutral mutations become substitutions at the rate they arise, whatever the population size. That steady input makes the clock tick.

scenes.tts: Now try to read a count as time. One distance could mean a fast rate over a short time. It could also mean a slow rate over a long time. The sequences alone cannot tell which.
scenes.visual: A single GOLD distance bar labelled 'same distance'. Above it, two tree pairs of equal total GOLD ticks: a short tree with ticks packed tightly (label 'fast rate, short time') and a tall tree with ticks spaced widely (label 'slow rate, long time'). A big '?' between them.
scenes.narration: Now try to read a count as time. One distance could mean a fast rate over a short time. It could also mean a slow rate over a long time. The sequences alone cannot tell which.

scenes.tts: You need one date from outside the sequences. The commonest is a fossil. If two splits share a rate, one dated split can date the other.
scenes.visual: A brown fossil stone drops onto the split of one tree pair; a date tag appears on its node. An arrow carries a 'shared rate' label from that pair to a second tree with no fossil, whose node then gets a computed date tag.
scenes.narration: You need one date from outside the sequences. The commonest is a fossil. If two splits share a rate, one dated split can date the other.

scenes.tts: But a fossil only shows the group existed by then. The real split was earlier, by an unknown margin. So a fossil gives a minimum age.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the fossil pin on the time axis. A shaded band extends below it (further back in time) with an arrow pointing earlier, labelled 'real split: somewhere earlier'. The fossil tag reads 'at least this old'.
scenes.narration: But a fossil only shows the group existed by then. The real split was earlier, by an unknown margin. So a fossil gives a minimum age.

scenes.tts: One limit already matters. The clock counts neutral changes. A mutation removed by selection never becomes a substitution, so a tightly constrained gene ticks slowly.
scenes.visual: Back to the population box: a new GOLD dot appears, flashes red and is crossed out ('removed by selection'), and no tick lands on the branch. Beside it, a second gene's tick track is sparse, labelled 'constrained gene: slow clock'.
scenes.narration: One limit already matters. The clock counts neutral changes. A mutation removed by selection never becomes a substitution, so a tightly constrained gene ticks slowly.

scenes.tts: So neutral changes pile up, on average, at the rate they arise. Count them, add one dated split, and the count becomes time.
scenes.visual: The full Y tree with even GOLD ticks on both branches, the fossil stone at one node with its 'at least' arrow, and a time axis in years appearing beside the tree.
scenes.narration: So neutral changes pile up, on average, at the rate they arise. Count them, add one dated split, and the count becomes time.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot. Line: 'Neutral changes tick at the mutation rate; one dated split reads time.'
